stories.headline: Iran official says support for new sanctions would be 'act of war,' other Middle East news
stories.title: Iran official says support for new sanctions would be 'act of war,' other Middle East news
stories.summary: Dubai, Aug 24: The new head of Iran's top security body warned Sunday that Tehran will see any country's support for new US economic measures against the Islamic Republic as an “act of war,” while Iran's president defended an MoU with the US. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday is expected to announce the new measures after the US vowed to impose an “unprecedented” level of economic warfare and isolation on a country that has lived for decades under sanctions. Also Monday, Pakistan's army chief is expected to visit Iran as mediators try to revive talks. Meanwhile, attacks calmed on the Strait of Hormuz, but posturing did not, as a recently created Iranian authority listed dozens of vessels it said will face restrictions on future transits. Here's a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Sunday. Full coverage can be found here. Iran's security chief sharpens warning to neighbours. The hard-line leader of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, issued his latest warning on X, with the comments quickly shared by Iranian state media. It came a day after Rezaei's most extensive public comments since being named to the post this month. “If (Trump) wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner,” he had told the state broadcaster in an interview that aired late Saturday. He said Iran would target other oil-shipping routes from the Persian Gulf — alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz. Rezaei, a former Revolutionary Guard commander and military adviser to Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, was part of senior appointments widely seen as hardening Tehran's political and military stance. Iranian president wants to move past neither war nor peace' Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian earlier Sunday said the memorandum of understanding signed in mid-June was the best way to move beyond a situation of “neither war nor peace," adding that Tehran can't attract investment nearly six months after the war began. “There is not a single provision in this agreement that amounts to capitulation,” Pezeshkian said in a speech published by state-run IRNA. “The supreme leader sets the policies, and we will follow that path.” The interim deal opened a 60-day period for talks aimed at ending the war and reaching an accord on Iran's nuclear program. That period ended last week with no signs of compromise or extension. No attacks confirmed on the strait, but new restrictions There were no confirmed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz over the past 48 hours, a multinational coalition overseen by the US Navy said Sunday, with shipping traffic still at reduced levels. The US military said its blockade of Iranian ports had redirected 70 commercial ships and disabled three as of Sunday. Iran's recently created Persian Gulf Strait Authority, sanctioned by the US, published a list of dozens of ships it said had violated arrangements for transiting the strait and would face future restrictions like fines or seizures. The strait had been considered an international waterway before the US and Israel attacked Iran on February 28. Iran and Oman, on the strait's other side, are now discussing management of it, which likely will include ships paying fees. Pakistan's army chief will visit Tehran Pakistani Field Marshal Asim Munir will lead a delegation to Tehran on Monday, Iranian state television reported, citing Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei. Two regional officials said the visit was part of Islamabad's efforts to de-escalate tensions between the United States and Iran and urge them to return to the negotiating table. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to discuss the matter publicly. Iran executes man arrested during January protests The Iranian judiciary's Mizan news agency reported the latest execution connected to nationwide protests early this year, saying Majid Adineh was arrested January 9 in Mohammadshahr, west of Tehran. The judiciary said forensic examinations indicated the handgun found on him had been fired on January 8-9. Mizan said Adineh had joined the unrest following calls by groups opposed to Iran's government and alleged that he had received training from groups outside the country. He was convicted under Iran's law imposing harsher penalties for espionage and cooperation with hostile states. Israeli settler arrested in beating of Palestinian amputee Police arrested a 16-year-old boy from the Israeli settlement of Avigayil in the beating of a 61-year-old Palestinian, Saeed Muhammad Ibrahim Rabah, outside his home in the occupied West Bank, a year after he lost a leg after being shot by a settler. Rabah told The Associated Press that the violence at his home in Khirbet al-Rakeez on Saturday was an effort to make families leave, but “we will remain, no matter what happens.” Separately, the West Bank Health Ministry said a 14-year-old in the Askar refugee camp in Nablus was shot dead by Israeli forces, who did not immediately comment. The uncle of Islam Maher Ajouri, Nehad Ajouri, called the shooting indiscriminate. And Israel's military said it detained a suspect in a stabbing attack that wounded a 24-year-old Israeli man in the area of al-Auja in the West Bank. Israel's emergency services said the man was in moderate condition. Airstrike in Gaza kills a four-year-old child Four-year-old Mohammed Taha died after an Israeli airstrike hit a central Gaza house on Sunday and wounded at least five others, according to the Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, which received the casualties. Israel's military later said it struck and killed a Hamas commander in central Gaza. The hospital confirmed that the man named Ismail Abu Ful was killed. An Israeli strike in southern Gaza wounded at least seven people, including three children, according to health officials at Nasser Hospital. The military did not immediately comment. And Defence Minister Israel Katz in a statement said he instructed the military to “act immediately and forcefully” to prevent launches of balloons, kites or drones from Gaza toward nearby Israeli communities. Before the October 7, 2023, attack by Hamas-led militants on Israel — when 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage — burning kites and balloons were sent from Gaza into southern Israel, causing fires and other damage. Hamas, in a statement Sunday, accused Israel of “using children's toys as a pretext” for attacks and further displacement of Gaza residents.

stories.headline: Let’s save Kashmir’s geological treasures from vandalisation!
stories.title: Let’s save Kashmir’s geological treasures from vandalisation!
stories.summary: Can you imagine how fast we are losing Karewas, which are geological and archeological repositories, being vandalised for earth excavation? 18 metric tons of clay, sand and bajri have been illegally excavated in Karewas of Budgam and Pulwama district in the last 5 years alone. The damage is far more than earth excavation. We need to understand that Karewas are not just raised mounds of earth. These Karewas were formed due to tectonic events which occured at different intervals during the uplift of the Pir Panjal Range due to Himalayan orogeny. Considered to be an important part of Kashmir’s eco-system. Karewas known as Wuder are a flat-topped tableland and consist of conglomerate, silt, clay, sands and lignite beds. What is important is that the climatic and tectonic record during the last 1.6 million years is well preserved in the sediments of Karewas of Kashmir valley. Years ago, fossils of Elephant species called Elephas hysudricus were found in Karewas of Pulwama and Budgam areas. Fossils of Sivatherium giganteum, an extinct species of Giraffe, have also been found in Samboora karewas near Pampore. Besides fish scales were found in Karewas of Gogjee Pathri and upper mountain areas of Liddermud and Yusmarg in Budgam district. Instead of taking measures to preserve these geological treasures, successive regimes have failed to stop earth mining in Karewas. Many karewas have been flattened by organised earth mafia using machines in Budgam and Pulwama districts. It is more concerning that excavated soil from these karewas has been mostly used in so-called developmental projects including construction of new roads in Kashmir and Railway projects. Wanton excavation of Karewas has led to soil erosion and extensive siltation of waterways and water bodies in Kashmir. Karewas help to retain rain water preventing flash floods and sudden rise in water levels in water bodies in its downstream areas. The massive destruction of Karewas prompted a noted environmental activist Dr Raja Muzaffar Bhat to approach the National Green Tribunal (NGT) stating that illegal clay, sand and bajri mining at Zadoora, Rangeen Kultreh villages of Pulwama and Chadoora Budgam had destroyed around 1000 kanals of land. This has led to immense loss to local apple, plum and almond orchards. The NGT constituted Joint Committee had in April this year visited the sites to ascertain the extent of illegal mining and the quantity of the clay and bajri which has been illegally extracted. The report of the Joint Committee comprising senior officers from Ministry of Environment Forest & Climate Change -MoEF, Central Pollution Control Board –CPCB, J&K Pollution Control Committee, Deputy Commissioners of Budgam and Pulwama has confirmed large scale illegal earth mining in karewas of Pulwama and Budgam in last 5 years. The report reveals that more than 18 lakh metric tons of clay ,sand , gravel has been illegally excavated in Zadoora , Gowherpora and Rangeen Kultreh villages of Pulwama and Budgam districts. Out of 18 lakh MTs , 130500 MTs of material has been excavated from Gowherpora and rangeen Kultreh villages of Chadoora Budgam and around 5 lakhs MTs from Zadoora village of Pulwama in Hastikhud area. The report quoting Mining Department J&K Government mentions that illegal excavation work took place due to law and order situation post article 370 abrogation and COVID 19 pandemic in 2020 and 2021. The report mentions that a company undertook earth mining at Gowherpora without any Environmental Clearance. A report filed by Ecology, Environment and Remote Sensing also confirms large scale mining has taken place as per satellite imagery between 2014 to 2026. The petitioner Dr Raja Muzaffar has sought a probe by CBI and ACB against the officials who allowed plunder of Karewas. Elsewhere in the world, efforts are being made to preserve mountains having geological importance. There are 241 UNESCO Global Geoparks in 51 countries. Global Geoparks (UGGp) are single, unified geographical areas where sites and landscapes of international geological significance are managed with a holistic concept of protection, education and sustainable development. UNESCO identifies regions with high-value geological features, mainly ancient mountain ranges, volcanoes, and fossils, making these eligible for inclusion in the Global Geoparks Network. UNESCO’s Global Geopark must demonstrate a geological heritage of international significance. The purpose of a UNESCO Global Geopark is to explore, develop and celebrate the links between that geological heritage and all other aspects of the area’s natural, cultural and intangible heritages. UNESCO aims at reconnecting human society at all levels to the planet to celebrate how our planet and its 4,600 million year long history has shaped every aspect of our lives and our societies. It is the duty of J&K Government and stakeholders to join hands and ensure Karewas of Kashmir gets global recognition by inclusion in UNESCO Global Geoparks network to ensure long term conservation and promotion. To begin with we have to save the remaining Karewas. Let the government begin with bringing strong legislation to prevent further excavation of Karewas and ensuring strict action against those who damage the natural creation. Even if we need soil for developmental works, let the government allow the sale of legally dredged soil from rivers. We must understand that the loss of Karewas is irreversible. Nothing can compensate for the loss of this natural creation. We must declare Karewas as heritage sites or natural museums. If we protect and preserve our Karewas, these can be a source of global research and be added to our tourism map. Kashmir’s Karewas offer massive scope for research as these are a valuable repository of the late Quaternary climatic changes and landscape evolution of Kashmir. Let’s act as guardians of our nature rather than its destroyers! Author is Executive Editor, Greater Kashmir

stories.headline: NSA Doval to visit China today to attend Special Representatives talks with FM Wang
stories.title: NSA Doval to visit China today to attend Special Representatives talks with FM Wang
stories.summary: National Security Advisor Ajit Doval is scheduled to arrive in Beijing on Monday to take part in the India-China Special Representatives (SR) talks on the boundary issue with his Chinese counterpart Wang Yi. Doval and Wang are scheduled to hold the 25th round of SR talks on Tuesday, according to official sources. Both Doval and Wang are the designated SRs for the boundary talks mechanism, which was established in 2003 to comprehensively address the vexed boundary dispute of the India-China border spanning 3,488 km. While success eluded it in resolving the boundary dispute, officials on both sides regard the structured mechanism as a useful tool in addressing the recurring tensions between the two countries on various fronts. The upcoming talks assume significance as they are being held ahead of the much-anticipated visit of Chinese President Xi Jinping to India to attend the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 12-13. While there is no official confirmation about Xi’s visit, officials on both sides are optimistic about the Chinese leader’s participation, which could provide an opportunity for a meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi on the sidelines of the summit to discuss initiatives to take forward bilateral ties. The two leaders met in August last year on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Tianjin. Ahead of Doval-Wang talks in Beijing, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on Saturday reiterated that peace and tranquillity along the border areas are prerequisite for good relations with China. His comments came amid reports of aggressive posturing by Chinese troops in Arunachal Pradesh's Upper Subansiri region in recent weeks. "I think we went through a particularly bad patch between the summer of 2020 and the autumn of 2024, and that was primarily an outcome of the situation in the border areas," Jaishankar said at the Economic Times World Leaders Forum in New Delhi on Saturday. "At the end of the day, peace and tranquillity in the border areas is a prerequisite for good relations, and the state of the border, to a very large measure, naturally would determine the state of the relations," he said. On the reports of stepped-up Chinese military activity near the Arunachal Pradesh border, China’s Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said on August 12 that the China-India border situation is "generally stable at the moment”. China and India held the 36th meeting of the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on China-India Border Affairs, Guo said. “The two sides agreed to maintain communication via diplomatic and military channels and jointly uphold peace and tranquility in the border areas”, he said. External Affairs Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal on August 11 said that India considers matters relating to border areas with China as "most serious" and asserted that maintaining peace and tranquillity along the Line of Actual Control (LAC) is of "utmost importance", as the state of the frontier will govern the overall trajectory of bilateral ties. Earlier, New Delhi also trashed Beijing's criticism of its decision to formally identify 27 places and geographical features in Arunachal Pradesh by their standard names, emphasising that the state is an "inalienable and integral" part of India and nothing can change this "indisputable reality". China, which claims Arunachal Pradesh as part of South Tibet, has been releasing its set of names for the region since 2017. India termed the Chinese move as "vain and preposterous", asserting that such actions will not alter the "undeniable" reality that the state "was, is, and will" always remain an integral part of India.

stories.headline: Hawkish MPC, West Asia conflict cloud rupee, bond yield outlook
stories.title: Hawkish MPC, West Asia conflict cloud rupee, bond yield outlook
stories.summary: Mumbai: Hawkish signals from the minutes of the latest monetary policy committee (MPC) review, escalation of the conflict in West Asia and the possibility of higher sugar imports are among the factors keeping the outlook for the rupee and bond yields clouded.What could be a mitigating factor, however, is the record haul from forex-inflow programs. India has so far received $72.8 billion in dollar inflows through the special swap facility, giving the central bank an additional buffer to manage pressure on the currency.133448778The rupee, aided by central bank interventions, is expected to trade between 95.50 and 96.00 levels, while the 10-year bond yield is expected to trade with a negative bias, around 6.85% levels."The minutes of the Monetary Policy Committee were more hawkish compared to the statements, so the market will take some time to adjust. The floor is 6.87% to 6.88% for the 10-year yield, and it will move upwards if there are more crude shocks. Additionally, global bonds, especially US rates, are also trading with a negative bias whose impact is felt domestically," said Gopal Tripathi, head of treasury, Jana Small Finance Bank.The August MPC minutes struck a more hawkish tone, with members flagging that a broadening of inflation pressures could warrant a rate hike or policy recalibration.Read more: FPIs invest Rs 23,544 crore in Indian equities in Aug on earnings revival, rupee stabilitySeparately, US Treasury yields initially fell sharply after the Treasury announced it would double its buybacks of longer-dated debt. After the buyback announcement on Thursday, the 10-year yield fell about 6 bps to 4.66%, while the 30-year dropped nearly 10 bps to 5.18%. But the rally quickly faded, by Friday, the US 10-year was back near 4.70% and the 30-year near 5.24%The 10 year India yield has decreased 28 bps to 6.85% this fiscal year.Oil PressureFor the rupee, oil prices remain a key pressure point even as the RBI continues to intervene. The intervention is expected to persist given the sizable inflows of $72.85 billion generated through the special swap facility, with $717 billion in foreign exchange reserves, traders said."Domestic markets' price action is likely to be more influenced by energy prices and US rate movements, with USDINR's attempts to break above 96.0 attracting strong counter presence of the RBI," said Radhika Rao, senior economist, DBS Bank.

stories.headline: EPG honours environmental champions, questions loss of open public spaces
stories.title: EPG honours environmental champions, questions loss of open public spaces
stories.summary: The Environmental Policy Group (EPG) on Saturday commemorated its departed co-founders and remembered its mentor and ideologue, late Syed Nassarullah Shah, on his fourth death anniversary at a function held at the Institution of Engineers, Srinagar. The annual function brought together members of civil society, academicians, lawyers, environmental activists and researchers to remember the contributions of those associated with the environmental movement and to recognise individuals who have made significant contributions towards environmental conservation and public causes. A seminar on the theme “Loss of Green/Open Spaces and Its Impact on Environment” was also held as part of the programme. Former Chairman of the Jammu and Kashmir Public Service Commission and former Commissioner-Secretary, General Administration Department, Farooq Ahmad Lone was the chief guest. A major highlight of the function was the recognition of environmental activist Abdul Hamid Bhat, CEO of Rahim Greens, for having planted a recorded 3.5 lakh saplings and plants. Bhat has set himself the ambitious target of planting one million trees. The EPG acknowledged Bhat’s contribution in the field of plantation and environmental conservation, particularly in view of the personal challenges he has faced. Bhat had suffered a serious accident after being hit by a truck while cycling on the Bypass around a year ago. He has since recovered to the extent of being able to walk with the support of a stick and a helper, while continuing his commitment to environmental conservation. In his welcome address, the EPG Convenor, Faiz Bakshi lauded environmental activists for continuing their conservation efforts despite difficult circumstances and expressed serious concern over the rapid disappearance of green and open spaces. He particularly referred to the proposed construction-related plans concerning the Polo Ground, describing the open space as a lifeline for thousands of youngsters who use it for sports, recreation and indoor games throughout the year. He cautioned that the loss of such spaces could deprive young people of healthy recreational outlets and make them more vulnerable to drug addiction and other social problems. Bakshi said the EPG had made several representations to the Government, from the Chief Minister to officials at lower levels of administration, but had not received a response. He added that efforts to obtain complete information through the Right to Information mechanism had also failed to provide clarity, leaving important details about the proposed interventions shrouded in secrecy. Referring to the chief guest's contribution as Deputy Commissioner, Srinagar, the Convenor recalled Farooq Ahmad Lone's role in allotting 32 kanals of land at Khonmoh for the Permian-Triassic Park.. He said the administrative decision had helped preserve fossils and a geological section associated with a significant global event in Earth's history. “If that decision had not been taken, the fossils and the section, which are a repository of a significant global event of the Great Dying, could have ended up being destroyed through stone mining, crushed aggregate and cement-related activity,” he said, saluting Lone for what he described as an administrative and historic act. Chairman of the EPG Legal Committee, Advocate Shafqat Nazir, dealt at length with the consequences of losing green and open spaces, particularly for young people. He argued that there should be more open spaces, playgrounds and sports infrastructure to provide young people with constructive alternatives to drugs. He pointed out what he described as a contradiction between policy declarations against drug addiction and the disappearance of spaces that provide opportunities for sports and recreation. Advocate Nazir said that if the Polo Ground gives way to a flyover, football, hockey and rugby grounds as well as the Sunday market would disappear. Referring to constitutional provisions and Supreme Court judgments, he spoke about the Government's obligation to protect public spaces, the environment and public health. He referred to the doctrine of public trust recognised in Supreme Court judgments, including those associated with V.S. Mutappa and M.C. Mehta, arguing that public resources such as land, water, forests and open spaces are held by the Government as a trustee for the public rather than as an absolute owner. He questioned whether stakeholders, including youngsters, Polo View shopkeepers and the Pollution Control Committee, had been consulted about the proposed project and, if so, why their feedback had not been made public. “The amount spent on the flyover will not buy us even ‘one Chinar’,” he concluded. Former Chief Town Planner Iftikhar Hakim, in his presentation, spoke about the loss of open and green spaces, wetlands and water bodies in Srinagar over the past several decades. He warned that allowing further construction on open spaces identified for protection under the Master Plan-2035 would undermine Srinagar's heritage character. Hakim also referred to the earth-filling of the Nowgam Flood Absorption Basin for setting up an industrial and warehousing area, despite restrictions on development and construction in the area under the Master Plan. He warned that continuing with such interventions could increase the city's vulnerability to flooding. Prof. Javed Hussain Mir of the Islamic University of Science and Technology spoke about the challenges facing the environment, natural resources and the livelihoods of citizens. Referring to various surveys and research findings, he highlighted the positive impact of green environments and plants on human well-being and stressed the importance of nature-based solutions for conservation of natural resources and improving human well-being. Chairman of the RTI Movement and Climate Action Group, Dr Raja Muzaffar Bhat, recalled his long association with late Syed Nassarullah Shah and paid tribute to his oratorical and drafting skills, crusading spirit and commitment to public causes. He described Shah as a fearless campaigner who was prepared to take on powerful interests in pursuit of people's and societal causes. He recalled his contribution to the human rights and Right to Information movements and said the best tribute to his memory would be to carry forward his legacy. Ajaz Rasool said that his association with Syed Nassarullah dated back to drafting the EPG flood-related PIL way back in 2015. He was very much impressed by his vocabulary and drafting skills. He added that environmental activists need to be more proactive if their efforts to conserve natural resources; otherwise, our future generations will curse us. Chief guest Farooq Ahmad Lone commended the EPG for organising the annual event in memory of Syed Nassarullah Shah, late Syed Abdul Rashid Shah and late Mohammad Ramzan Khan (Gurezi), who had co-founded the Environmental Policy Group and contributed to its activities. He said the well-being of the environment was intrinsically linked to the well-being of society and observed that the presentations made during the function were particularly relevant in the context of climate change and global warming. Lone congratulated the awardees and described them as crusaders for environmental protection. He was felicitated with a Chinar, the emblem of Kashmir, carved out of walnut wood. The EPG also honoured late Syed Abdul Rashid Shah, Co-founder and Trustee of EPG, posthumously, with the award being received by his family members. Late G.H. Kango, former PCCF Forests and Chairman PEC, was also honoured posthumously, with family members receiving the recognition. Other awardees and recipients of mementoes included Er. Iftikhar Hakim, Prof. Javed Hussain Mir, Syed Sammi Nassarullah Shah, Advocates Shafqat Nazir and Shabir A. Bhat of the EPG Legal Team, Dr Raja Muzaffar Bhat, Er. Ajaz Rasool, Dr G.N. Qasba, Gowhar Maqbool, Advocate Rasikh Rasool, Ajaz Ahmad Dar, Rauf Tramboo, Shahala Sheikh and Faiz Bakshi. In his vote of thanks, EPG Co-Convenor Dr M.M. Shuja thanked the chief guest and participants for attending the programme. Remembering Syed Nassarullah Shah as a powerful voice for society, human rights, the RTI movement, environmental protection and social causes, Dr Shuja said he had also been a champion of public interest litigation and had drafted more than two dozen PILs. He recalled the last words spoken to him by Shah around two hours before his death: “Follow the PILs and petitions — strengthen the organisation — continue service to society.” The programme was anchored by EPG Co-founder and Trustee Peerzada Fayaz Ahmad, while the award ceremony was conducted by Dr Tauseef Bhat, EPG Co-founder and Trustee, who also recalled his long association with Syed Nassarullah Shah and Syed Abdul Rashid Shah.

stories.headline: NC made promises it could never fulfil: Akhoon
stories.title: NC made promises it could never fulfil: Akhoon
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 23: Jammu and Kashmir Apni Party State Vice President Mohammad Syed Akhoon on Sunday launched a sharp attack on the ruling National Conference (NC), alleging that the party has “reduced itself to a power-hungry organisation” and accusing it of misleading people with promises he claimed were unrealistic and difficult to fulfil. Addressing a public gathering at Brein-Nishat in Srinagar, chaired by Apni Party president Syed Mohammad Altaf Bukhari, Akhoon said his decision to leave the NC after decades of association had surprised many people. Taking aim at his former party, Akhoon alleged that the NC had become more focused on retaining power than addressing the dignity, aspirations and day-to-day concerns of the people. Recalling his association with the NC, Akhoon said he had openly opposed what he described as “unrealistic” promises made in the party’s election manifesto. He claimed that he had raised his concerns during a working committee meeting attended by senior leaders, including Dr Farooq Abdullah and Omar Abdullah. Akhoon said he had specifically questioned the feasibility of promises relating to enhanced ration, 12 LPG cylinders, 200 units of free electricity and one lakh jobs. “I told them we should not make promises that cannot be fulfilled. We should not mislead people,” he said, claiming that he subsequently faced action after expressing similar views publicly. Akhoon said he had remained associated with the National Conference since 1967 and had worked alongside several senior leaders during his long political career. He said he eventually decided to leave the party after concluding that it had drifted away from the principles with which he had been associated. He also criticised the state of civic infrastructure in Srinagar, alleging that residents in the city’s core areas continue to face inadequate basic amenities. Akhoon claimed that some remote and mountainous areas have better civic facilities than several localities in the heart of Srinagar. Explaining his decision to join the Apni Party, Akhoon said he had spent nearly two years assessing the political situation before taking the decision. “I spent nearly two years assessing the political situation before taking the step. I found Altaf Bukhari to be an honest leader committed to addressing unemployment and the everyday concerns of the people,” he said. Akhoon also defended Bukhari against allegations levelled against him by political opponents, describing the Apni Party president as a self-made individual with an established family background and rejecting claims that he required support from any outside agency. Referring to the recent increase in electricity tariffs, Akhoon accused the NC government of failing to honour its promise of providing 200 units of free electricity. He said the tariff increase had instead added to the financial burden on economically weaker sections. Akhoon also criticised what he described as the NC’s internal approach to political representation. Referring to the Independence Day function, he alleged that elected legislators were overlooked while prominence was given to a defeated candidate, which he said reflected the party’s priorities. He further alleged that several individuals currently holding important positions in the NC belonged to families that had “backstabbed” Sheikh Mohammad Abdullah in the past and contributed to his imprisonment. Appealing to people to strengthen the Apni Party, Akhoon urged voters to support Altaf Bukhari’s leadership for addressing unemployment and other public issues. He also claimed that people attending the rally had gathered voluntarily and without monetary inducements, contrasting it with what he alleged was the practice of some political parties of mobilising crowds through financial incentives.

stories.headline: Industries face nearly 10% power tariff hike
stories.title: Industries face nearly 10% power tariff hike
stories.summary: Srinagar, Aug 23: The latest revision in electricity tariffs is set to raise the principal energy charges for industrial consumers in Jammu and Kashmir by nearly 10 percent, adding to the cost pressures confronting manufacturers at a time when the government is working on measures to revive existing industrial units. The increase is significantly higher than the 6.83 percent average tariff revision announced by the Joint Electricity Regulatory Commission (JERC). The revised tariff, approved through Order No 06 of 2026 on August 20, will apply from September 1. For LTIS-I industrial consumers, the energy charge has been raised from Rs 4.20 to Rs 4.60 per kVAh, translating into an increase of 9.52 percent. For HT industrial consumers at 11 kV, the rate has gone up from Rs 4.10 to Rs 4.50 per kVAh, an increase of 9.76 percent. Industrialists say the impact will not be confined to the headline energy charge, as fixed and demand charges have also been revised, potentially increasing the overall electricity expenditure of manufacturing units. The Federation of Chambers of Industries Kashmir (FCIK) has opposed the increase and sought intervention by Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, arguing that the actual burden on industry is considerably higher than the average figure being cited. A representative of FCIK said the distinction was important because industrial consumers were facing a substantially higher increase than the average tariff revision. "For industry, 6.83 percent is therefore not the real story. More inexplicable is that KPDCL and JPDCL themselves sought only a 5 percent across-the-board increase, whereas JERC has imposed an increase approaching twice that percentage on the principal industrial energy charge,” the FCIK representative said. The concern comes against the backdrop of efforts to revive existing industrial units, many of which are reportedly operating below capacity and facing high input and transportation costs. A Kashmir-based industrialist said electricity was among the basic recurring costs that directly affected the viability of manufacturing units. “Electricity is not an optional expense for industry. Every increase in the power bill directly adds to the cost of production. When a unit is already operating below capacity, absorbing another substantial increase becomes extremely difficult,” he said. Another industrialist said the problem was particularly acute for units competing with manufacturers from outside J&K. “Our products have to compete with goods coming from areas where industries have better logistics, larger markets and often lower operating costs. If our electricity, freight and raw-material costs continue to rise, our competitiveness will suffer further,” he said. Industrial stakeholders have also questioned the rationale for passing system-wide distribution losses on to industrial consumers, particularly where consumption is metered. FCIK has argued that HT industrial consumers are subject to precise energy and demand metering and that losses arising from theft, unmetered consumption, deficient billing and poor recoveries elsewhere in the distribution system should not automatically become a liability for industries. A representative of an industrial unit said the issue was not about seeking preferential treatment but about ensuring that efficient consumers were not made to pay for inefficiencies beyond their control. “If an industrial unit is being billed on the basis of actual metered consumption and is paying its dues, it is difficult to understand why it should also carry the cost of electricity that is lost, stolen or not recovered elsewhere,” he said. FCIK has also questioned the distribution-loss assumptions used in the tariff determination, including figures of around 15 percent for JPDCL and 19 percent for KPDCL. The federation has sought greater transparency regarding where these losses occur and how much is attributable to technical losses, theft, unmetered consumption and commercial inefficiencies. FCIK has also raised concerns over the consultation process preceding the tariff order. According to the federation, the distribution companies had proposed an across-the-board increase of 5 percent, while the final increase in the principal industrial energy charge was close to 10 percent. An industrialist said the difference deserved closer examination. “If stakeholders were responding to a proposal for a 5 percent increase, but the final order imposes almost twice that increase on a particular industrial category, there should have been a clear opportunity for that category to respond to the higher proposed burden,” he said. The tariff revision has also revived concerns about the broader cost structure facing J&K's industrial sector. Industrialists cite high freight charges, the distance from major markets and raw-material sources, difficult terrain and, in Kashmir, a relatively limited working season as factors that already raise production costs. “An industrial unit in Kashmir does not operate in the same environment as a unit located close to a major industrial or consumption centre. opening: Srinagar, Aug 23: The latest revision in electricity tariffs is set to raise the principal energy charges for industrial consumers in Jammu and Kashmir by nearly 10 percent, adding to the cost pressures confronting manufacturers at a time when the government is working on measures to revive existing industrial units.
The revised tariff, approved through Order No 06 of 2026 on August 20, will apply from September 1.
body: Industrialists say the impact will not be confined to the headline energy charge, as fixed and demand charges have also been revised, potentially increasing the overall electricity expenditure of manufacturing units.

The Federation of Chambers of Industries Kashmir (FCIK) has opposed the increase and sought intervention by Chief Minister Omar Abdullah, arguing that the actual burden on industry is considerably higher than the average figure being cited.
A representative of FCIK said the distinction was important because industrial consumers were facing a substantially higher increase than the average tariff revision.
"For industry, 6.83 percent is therefore not the real story.
The concern comes against the backdrop of efforts to revive existing industrial units, many of which are reportedly operating below capacity and facing high input and transportation costs.
A Kashmir-based industrialist said electricity was among the basic recurring costs that directly affected the viability of manufacturing units.
“Electricity is not an optional expense for industry.
Every increase in the power bill directly adds to the cost of production.
When a unit is already operating below capacity, absorbing another substantial increase becomes extremely difficult,” he said.

Another industrialist said the problem was particularly acute for units competing with manufacturers from outside J&K. “Our products have to compete with goods coming from areas where industries have better logistics, larger markets and often lower operating costs.
If our electricity, freight and raw-material costs continue to rise, our competitiveness will suffer further,” he said.
Industrial stakeholders have also questioned the rationale for passing system-wide distribution losses on to industrial consumers, particularly where consumption is metered.

FCIK has argued that HT industrial consumers are subject to precise energy and demand metering and that losses arising from theft, unmetered consumption, deficient billing and poor recoveries elsewhere in the distribution system should not automatically become a liability for industries.

A representative of an industrial unit said the issue was not about seeking preferential treatment but about ensuring that efficient consumers were not made to pay for inefficiencies beyond their control.

“If an industrial unit is being billed on the basis of actual metered consumption and is paying its dues, it is difficult to understand why it should also carry the cost of electricity that is lost, stolen or not recovered elsewhere,” he said.
FCIK has also questioned the distribution-loss assumptions used in the tariff determination, including figures of around 15 percent for JPDCL and 19 percent for KPDCL.
The federation has sought greater transparency regarding where these losses occur and how much is attributable to technical losses, theft, unmetered consumption and commercial inefficiencies.
FCIK has also raised concerns over the consultation process preceding the tariff order.

According to the federation, the distribution companies had proposed an across-the-board increase of 5 percent, while the final increase in the principal industrial energy charge was close to 10 percent.
An industrialist said the difference deserved closer examination.
The tariff revision has also revived concerns about the broader cost structure facing J&K's industrial sector.

Industrialists cite high freight charges, the distance from major markets and raw-material sources, difficult terrain and, in Kashmir, a relatively limited working season as factors that already raise production costs.
“An industrial unit in Kashmir does not operate in the same environment as a unit located close to a major industrial or consumption centre.
Transporting raw material in and finished products out is already expensive.
Power costs are another major component.
When these costs rise simultaneously, the pressure eventually reflects either in prices, lower production or employment,” another industrialist said.

FCIK has accordingly called for greater scrutiny of the components underlying the tariff determination, including power purchase and transmission costs, procurement efficiency, operation and maintenance expenditure, bad debts, collection shortfalls and non-tariff revenues.
The federation has also pointed to the Commission's previous observation that distribution losses are a controllable parameter and that inefficiencies should not be passed on to consumers.

The industrial body has urged the Power Development Department, JPDCL, and KPDCL to seek review and reconsideration of JERC Order No 06 of 2026 and restore the pre-order tariff for existing industrial consumers.
Industrialists say the tariff increase should therefore be examined in the broader context of industrial revival rather than as an isolated revision.
“Revival of industry and escalation of its basic input costs cannot travel together.
If the objective is to revive existing units, every major increase in the cost of production needs to be carefully examined,” an industrialist said.

FCIK has appealed to Chief Minister Omar Abdullah to intervene before the revised tariff begins putting additional pressure on existing enterprises and has sought that the enhanced industrial rates be kept in abeyance pending review by JERC.
